slides.headline: In one sentence
slides.body: gh is a client for GitHub's API that knows which repository you're in, so the GitHub objects become reachable from the directory where your Git data is.

slides.headline: Precisely
slides.body: gh isn't Git and doesn't replace it.

client                         credential it presents                    one API

   | gh          | ---- acts as you, everywhere you have ----> | GitHub's API   |

slides.headline: Step 2: the release command explains itself

lines.s: gh release create --help | sed -n '/^If a matching git tag/,/^If the tag is not annotated/p'
If a matching git tag does not yet exist, one will automatically get created
from the latest state of the default branch.
Use `--target` to point to a different branch or commit for the automatic tag creation.
Use `--verify-tag` to abort the release if the tag doesn't already exist.
To fetch the new tag locally after the release, do `git fetch --tags origin`.
To create a release from an annotated git tag, first create one locally with
git, push the tag to GitHub, then run this command.
Use `--notes-from-tag` to get the release notes from the annotated git tag.
If the tag is not annotated, the commit message will be used instead.
-d, --draft                        Save the release as a draft instead of publishing it
--generate-notes               Automatically generate title and notes for the release via GitHub
--notes-from-tag               Fetch notes from the tag annotation or message of commit associated
-p, --prerelease                   Mark the release as a prerelease
--target branch                Target branch or full commit SHA (default [main branch])
--verify-tag                   Abort in case the git tag doesn't already exist in the remote
--cleanup-tag   Delete the specified tag in addition to its release
-F, --field key=value       Add a typed parameter in key=value format (use "@<path>" or "@-" to read
-H, --header key:value      Add a HTTP request header in key:value format
--hostname string       The GitHub hostname for the request (default "github.com")
-i, --include               Include HTTP response status line and headers in the output
--input file            The file to use as body for the HTTP request (use "-" to read from standard
-q, --jq string             Query to select values from the response using jq syntax
-X, --method string         The HTTP method for the request (default "GET")
--paginate              Make additional HTTP requests to fetch all pages of results
-p, --preview strings       Opt into GitHub API previews (names should omit '-preview')
-f, --raw-field key=value   Add a string parameter in key=value format
--silent                Do not print the response body
--slurp                 Use with "--paginate" to return an array of all pages of either JSON arrays
-t, --template string       Format JSON output using a Go template; see "gh help formatting"
--verbose               Include full HTTP request and response in the output
check:         View rules that would apply to a given branch
list:          List rulesets for a repository or organization
view:          View information about a ruleset

slides.body: git push: Git data on the server.
Five mistakes to watch for.

items: A script reports exactly 30 items. Root cause: lists return 30 items per page and the script did not pass --paginate.
A script created something by accident. Root cause: a field flag switched the method from GET to POST; -X GET keeps it a read.
gh acts on the wrong one of fork and upstream. Root cause: with two remotes there are two candidates, and no default was recorded with gh repo set-default.
Reading a 404 as "the repository does not exist". Root cause: for a private resource and a token without access the API answers 404 on purpose.

Building tooling on a personal token and on human-readable output. Root cause: the token acts as one person everywhere and stops when that person leaves, and the text output is not a stable interface; use --json, the version header, and a GitHub App.

slides.body: Read sections 15.16 to 15.18 and 15.20 to 15.22 of Chapter 15, and section 17.16 of Chapter 17. Do Lab 25.2, "Queries with gh api", in lab-manual/m25-github-cli-api.md.
Today you took the CLI apart into its Git half and its GitHub half, and you met the two defaults that surprise every script once.

beats.text: Both come from one script, written in an afternoon, that calls gh api in a loop. gh is GitHub's command-line program, and gh api sends a request to GitHub's API, the interface that programs use to talk to GitHub. Nobody intended either result. The first is a default of the API. The second is a default of the CLI: one flag changed the HTTP method, the verb of the request, without the author noticing.

beats.text: If you're going to automate anything on GitHub, and on an AI and ML team you will, you need to know what the CLI does on your behalf. This video gives you that, and the two defaults behind those two lines. Keep both lines in mind. Each gets its explanation.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. Through Part 5 you've used gh in almost every lab without a formal introduction. This video is that introduction, and it closes the GitHub part before the gate.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. Through Part 5 you've used `gh` in almost every lab without a formal introduction. This video is that introduction, and it closes the GitHub part before the gate.

beats.text: Four topics. First, what gh is: a client of GitHub's API that knows which repository you're in. Second, gh pr: a full pull request cycle from the terminal, and which of its commands change state. A pull request is GitHub's proposal to merge one branch into another. Third, gh api: the REST API, its method, fields, pagination and version header, then GraphQL at concept level, and rate limits. Fourth, the integration model: webhooks and GitHub Apps, and when an integration should be an App and not your personal token.

Second, `gh pr`: a full pull request cycle from the terminal, and which of its commands change state. A pull request is GitHub's proposal to merge one branch into another. Third, `gh api`: the REST API, its method, fields, pagination and version header, then GraphQL at concept level, and rate limits. Fourth, the integration model: webhooks and GitHub Apps, and when an integration should be an App and not your personal token.

beats.text: In one sentence. gh is a client for GitHub's API that knows which repository you're in, so the GitHub objects become reachable from the directory where your Git data is.
beats.tele: In one sentence. `gh` is a client for GitHub's API that knows which repository you're in, so the GitHub objects become reachable from the directory where your Git data is.

beats.text: Precisely. gh isn't Git and doesn't replace it. It calls the REST and GraphQL APIs with a stored token, a string that stands for your account with a subset of its rights. It runs git for you where a task needs both, as in gh repo clone and gh pr checkout. And it can act as Git's credential helper.
beats.tele: Precisely. `gh` isn't Git and doesn't replace it. It calls the REST and GraphQL APIs with a stored token, a string that stands for your account with a subset of its rights. It runs `git` for you where a task needs both, as in `gh repo clone` and `gh pr checkout`. And it can act as Git's credential helper.

beats.text: Four behaviors explain most surprises.
beats.tele: Four behaviors explain most surprises.

beats.text: Which repository? Inside a clone, gh picks the repository from your remotes. With a fork there are two candidates, and gh repo set-default records which one to use. Outside a clone, or to override, you pass -R with owner and repository, or set GH_REPO.
beats.tele: Which repository? Inside a clone, `gh` picks the repository from your remotes. With a fork there are two candidates, and `gh repo set-default` records which one to use. Outside a clone, or to override, you pass `-R` with owner and repository, or set `GH_REPO`.

beats.text: Machine-readable output. Most listing commands take --json with a list of fields, then --jq with an expression, or --template. JSON is a text format for structured data. --json without a field list prints the available fields.
beats.tele: Machine-readable output. Most listing commands take `--json` with a list of fields, then `--jq` with an expression, or `--template`. JSON is a text format for structured data. `--json` without a field list prints the available fields.

beats.text: Exit codes. 0 for success, 1 for failure, 2 when cancelled, 4 when authentication is required. gh pr checks adds 8 for pending checks. Scripts should test exit codes and not parse human-readable output.
beats.tele: Exit codes. 0 for success, 1 for failure, 2 when cancelled, 4 when authentication is required. `gh pr checks` adds 8 for pending checks. Scripts should test exit codes and not parse human-readable output.

beats.text: Its own token. GH_TOKEN in the environment takes precedence over the stored login. A stale one in a shell profile explains "gh works in one terminal and not in another".
beats.tele: Its own token. `GH_TOKEN` in the environment takes precedence over the stored login. A stale one in a shell profile explains "gh works in one terminal and not in another".

beats.text: gh pr. In one sentence: gh pr drives the pull request object from the terminal. The Git work around it stays with git.

beats.text: Now the labels, because this is the objective people skip. gh pr view, gh pr checks, gh pr diff and gh pr status read: 🟢 SAFE. gh pr checkout is 🟢 SAFE too. It changes local files and refs only. gh pr create is 🟡 CAUTION: it may push the branch, and it creates a GitHub object that notifies people.
beats.tele: Now the labels, because this is the objective people skip. `gh pr view`, `gh pr checks`, `gh pr diff` and `gh pr status` read: 🟢 SAFE. `gh pr checkout` is 🟢 SAFE too. It changes local files and refs only. `gh pr create` is 🟡 CAUTION: it may push the branch, and it creates a GitHub object that notifies people.

beats.text: The preview is --dry-run, and the textbook notes that even the dry run may still push. gh pr merge, gh pr update-branch and gh pr edit --base are 🟡 CAUTION: they write to the base branch, move the head branch or change the base, and they can dismiss approvals.

beats.text: One flag is 🔴 DANGEROUS: gh pr merge --admin. What it changes: the base branch, without the required reviews or checks. What it can destroy: no data. What's lost is the review and the checks that the rules required. Preview: gh pr checks --required. Recovery: gh pr revert, and record the reason. Appropriate: a documented emergency, by someone the bypass list names.

beats.text: Two details from the help text. gh pr create takes the base from --base, else from a Git configuration value for the current branch, else the default branch. And --match-head-commit merges only if the head is the given commit: you merge what you reviewed, and not what was pushed a second ago.

And `--match-head-commit` merges only if the head is the given commit: you merge what you reviewed, and not what was pushed a second ago.

beats.text: gh api. In one sentence: everything GitHub shows you comes from an API that you can call yourself. gh api adds your token, the host and the placeholders, and prints the JSON.
beats.tele: `gh api`. In one sentence: everything GitHub shows you comes from an API that you can call yourself. `gh api` adds your token, the host and the placeholders, and prints the JSON.

beats.text: The REST API is a set of URLs, one per resource. gh api takes the path and fills in the placeholders for owner, repository and branch from the current repository.
beats.tele: The REST API is a set of URLs, one per resource. `gh api` takes the path and fills in the placeholders for owner, repository and branch from the current repository.

beats.text: Five rules of the road.
beats.tele: Five rules of the road.

beats.text: First, a quick quiz. A GET request reads, and a POST creates. You call gh api to list issues, and you add one filter with -f. What does the CLI send? A, a GET with a filter. B, a POST. Your answer?
beats.tele: First, a quick quiz. A `GET` request reads, and a `POST` creates. You call `gh api` to list issues, and you add one filter with `-f`. What does the CLI send? A, a `GET` with a filter. B, a `POST`. Your answer?

beats.text: B, a POST. Method. GET by default, and POST as soon as you add a field with -f or -F. To send parameters with a GET, you say -X GET. That's the second line of the hook: a filter parameter turned a read into a create.
beats.tele: B, a `POST`. Method. `GET` by default, and `POST` as soon as you add a field with `-f` or `-F`. To send parameters with a `GET`, you say `-X GET`. That's the second line of the hook: a filter parameter turned a read into a create.

beats.text: Fields. -f sends a string. -F converts true, false, null and integers to JSON types and can read a file.
beats.tele: Fields. `-f` sends a string. `-F` converts `true`, `false`, `null` and integers to JSON types and can read a file.

beats.text: Pagination. Lists return 30 items per page unless you ask otherwise. --paginate follows the pages. --slurp wraps them into one array. That's the first line of the hook.
beats.tele: Pagination. Lists return 30 items per page unless you ask otherwise. `--paginate` follows the pages. `--slurp` wraps them into one array. That's the first line of the hook.

beats.text: Versioning. The REST API is versioned by date through the X-GitHub-Api-Version header. Without the header, a request gets version 2022-11-28, which is supported until the tenth of March 2028. 2026-03-10 is the first version with breaking changes. An unsupported version answers 410 Gone. The CLI pins its own REST calls to 2022-11-28 since version 2.87.0. In a script that must keep working, send the header explicitly.
beats.tele: Versioning. The REST API is versioned by date through the `X-GitHub-Api-Version` header. Without the header, a request gets version `2022-11-28`, which is supported until the tenth of March 2028. `2026-03-10` is the first version with breaking changes. An unsupported version answers `410 Gone`. The CLI pins its own REST calls to `2022-11-28` since version 2.87.0. In a script that must keep working, send the header explicitly.

beats.text: Not found means "not for you". For a private resource and a token without access, the API answers 404, not 403, in the documentation's words "to avoid confirming the existence of private repositories".
beats.tele: Not found means "not for you". For a private resource and a token without access, the API answers `404`, not `403`, in the documentation's words "to avoid confirming the existence of private repositories".

beats.text: Every gh api call with GET is 🟢 SAFE. Every call with POST, PATCH, PUT or DELETE, and every GraphQL mutation, is 🔴 DANGEROUS, and section 15.22 gives the reason in one line: it changes whatever the endpoint says, with all your permissions. The preview is always the GET first. The recovery depends on the endpoint, and often there's none.
beats.tele: Every `gh api` call with `GET` is 🟢 SAFE. Every call with `POST`, `PATCH`, `PUT` or `DELETE`, and every GraphQL mutation, is 🔴 DANGEROUS, and section 15.22 gives the reason in one line: it changes whatever the endpoint says, with all your permissions. The preview is always the `GET` first. The recovery depends on the endpoint, and often there's none.

beats.text: GraphQL is the second API: one endpoint, a typed schema, and a query that names exactly the fields wanted, so one call can replace several REST requests. gh api graphql -f query= followed by the query calls it. A GraphQL query only reads, although it's sent as a POST. Some features exist in only one of the two APIs.
beats.tele: GraphQL is the second API: one endpoint, a typed schema, and a query that names exactly the fields wanted, so one call can replace several REST requests. `gh api graphql -f query=` followed by the query calls it. A GraphQL query only reads, although it's sent as a `POST`. Some features exist in only one of the two APIs.

beats.text: Rate limits. With no authentication: 60 requests per hour, per IP address. An authenticated user, which is your token and gh: 5,000 per hour. A GitHub App installation: 5,000 per hour at minimum, 15,000 on Enterprise Cloud organizations. The GITHUB_TOKEN in a workflow: 1,000 requests per hour per repository.
beats.tele: Rate limits. With no authentication: 60 requests per hour, per IP address. An authenticated user, which is your token and `gh`: 5,000 per hour. A GitHub App installation: 5,000 per hour at minimum, 15,000 on Enterprise Cloud organizations. The `GITHUB_TOKEN` in a workflow: 1,000 requests per hour per repository.

beats.text: Secondary limits apply on top: at most 100 concurrent requests, and a points budget per minute. Exceeding a limit returns 403 or 429. So a 403 isn't always a permission problem. gh api rate_limit tells you where you stand.
beats.tele: Secondary limits apply on top: at most 100 concurrent requests, and a points budget per minute. Exceeding a limit returns `403` or `429`. So a `403` isn't always a permission problem. `gh api rate_limit` tells you where you stand.

beats.text: Webhooks and GitHub Apps. Polling asks GitHub repeatedly whether something happened. A webhook reverses the direction: you register a URL and the events you care about, and GitHub sends an HTTP request with a JSON payload when one occurs. A push webhook carries the ref and the commit IDs before and after the push. The textbook's remark is worth repeating: that's the information of a reflog line, delivered to your server.
beats.tele: Webhooks and GitHub Apps. Polling asks GitHub repeatedly whether something happened. A webhook reverses the direction: you register a URL and the events you care about, and GitHub sends an HTTP request with a JSON payload when one occurs. A `push` webhook carries the ref and the commit IDs before and after the push. The textbook's remark is worth repeating: that's the information of a reflog line, delivered to your server.

beats.text: A GitHub App is the identity an integration should have. It's installed on chosen repositories. It holds fine-grained permissions. It receives webhooks. It acts with installation tokens that expire after one hour. And it isn't tied to a person, so it doesn't stop working when someone leaves.
beats.tele: A GitHub App is the identity an integration should have. It's installed on chosen repositories. It holds fine-grained permissions. It receives webhooks. It acts with installation tokens that expire after one hour. And it isn't tied to a person, so it doesn't stop working when someone leaves.

beats.text: The alternatives are a personal token, which acts as you everywhere you have access, and a machine user. One fact for tool writers: the API for check runs and check suites is available only to GitHub Apps. The older commit statuses can be created with Write access.
beats.tele: The alternatives are a personal token, which acts as you everywhere you have access, and a machine user. One fact for tool writers: the API for check runs and check suites is available only to GitHub Apps. The older commit statuses can be created with Write access.

beats.text: One thing here is unverified. Webhook delivery retries and signature validation weren't researched for the Phase 0 report, and aren't described in the course.

beats.text: There's one API. Everything else is a client.
beats.tele: There's one API. Everything else is a client.

beats.text: The browser is a client. gh is a client. A script with curl is a client. A GitHub App is a client. What differs between them is the credential each presents, and therefore what each may do and how often.
beats.tele: The browser is a client. `gh` is a client. A script with `curl` is a client. A GitHub App is a client. What differs between them is the credential each presents, and therefore what each may do and how often.

beats.text: So for any automation question, ask three things in this order. Which endpoint am I calling, and with which method? Which credential is making the call, and what else can that credential do? And what happens to this automation when the person who wrote it changes teams?
beats.tele: So for any automation question, ask three things in this order. Which endpoint am I calling, and with which method? Which credential is making the call, and what else can that credential do? And what happens to this automation when the person who wrote it changes teams?

beats.text: The model breaks slightly for gh, because gh is two clients in one. It talks to the API, and it also runs git on your machine.

beats.text: Read the first sentence of the help text aloud: if a matching Git tag doesn't yet exist, one will automatically get created from the latest state of the default branch. The textbook's production case: a release script on the day the version variable holds a typo. --verify-tag turns that into an error before anything is created.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: A script reports exactly 30 items. Root cause: lists return 30 items per page and the script did not pass --paginate.

beats.text: A script created something by accident. Root cause: a field flag switched the method from GET to POST; -X GET keeps it a read.
beats.tele: A script created something by accident. Root cause: a field flag switched the method from `GET` to `POST`; `-X GET` keeps it a read.

beats.text: gh acts on the wrong one of fork and upstream. Root cause: with two remotes there are two candidates, and no default was recorded with gh repo set-default.
beats.tele: `gh` acts on the wrong one of fork and upstream. Root cause: with two remotes there are two candidates, and no default was recorded with `gh repo set-default`.

beats.text: Reading a 404 as "the repository does not exist". Root cause: for a private resource and a token without access the API answers 404 on purpose.
beats.tele: Reading a `404` as "the repository does not exist". Root cause: for a private resource and a token without access the API answers `404` on purpose.

beats.text: Building tooling on a personal token and on human-readable output. Root cause: the token acts as one person everywhere and stops when that person leaves, and the text output is not a stable interface; use --json, the version header, and a GitHub App.
beats.tele: Building tooling on a personal token and on human-readable output. Root cause: the token acts as one person everywhere and stops when that person leaves, and the text output is not a stable interface; use `--json`, the version header, and a GitHub App.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. The textbook's case. A nightly job lists the pull requests of sixty repositories with unauthenticated curl. It worked from a laptop. It fails on the shared CI runner, where the sixty requests per hour of that IP address are spent before the job starts. Unauthenticated limits were lowered on the eighth of May 2025, anonymous HTTPS clones included.
beats.tele: Now, out of the lab. The textbook's case. A nightly job lists the pull requests of sixty repositories with unauthenticated `curl`. It worked from a laptop. It fails on the shared CI runner, where the sixty requests per hour of that IP address are spent before the job starts. Unauthenticated limits were lowered on the eighth of May 2025, anonymous HTTPS clones included.

says: Sixty repositories, and 60 requests per hour for that IP address

beats.text: The tempting repair is a retry loop. The textbook's verdict: the fix is an identity for the job, not a retry loop. For an evaluation dashboard on an AI and ML team that reads pull request data every night, the identity is a GitHub App installed on those sixty repositories with read permission for pull requests. The job then has its own rate limit, and it survives the departure of whoever wrote it.
